newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: OPINION - From the Beehive-Nats' chances strengthen.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - From the Beehive-Nats' chances strengthen.

text.p: WELLINGTON, Nov 20 - Winston Peters dismisses it as "mindless unsubstantiated speculation", but nevertheless the prospect of NZ First going into coalition with National, rather than Labour, has strengthened.
Labour leader Helen Clark attributes the speculation to National's "spin doctors", and detects signs of panic within National's ranks.
She believes National's Jim Bolger and Bill Birch are desperate to hold on to power, and will do anything to secure a deal with Peters.
The test may come over the finance portfolio.
According to Michael Laws, the logical choice for Finance Minister in a coalition will be Winston Peters.
Clark says however that she stands by her pre-election statement that in a Labour-led coalition, Labour's deputy leader Michael Cullen would be finance minister, and that was non-negotiable.

National, too, would be reluctant to yield the finance portfolio, particularly if it meant the sacrifice of Bill Birch. The solution may come in a variation of the Australian theme, where the Federal Cabinet in Canberra has both a Treasurer and a
Finance Minister. Or it could come with the allocation of a key cabinet committee chairmanship to Peters.

Meanwhile National backbencher Nick Smith has given a clue on how he thinks coalition talks are going. NZ First, he says, had come to realise the problems it would face with a three-party coalition including the Alliance, and so the talks with National had become more realistic.
He says such a deal would involve compromises and he would be in favour of dumping the second round of tax cuts if it meant more money could be spent on health, education and social welfare.
"In my view that should take priority over the second round of tax cuts."

The hard choices, he added, were going to be over increasing expenditure, tax cuts, repaying debt, and maintaining economic performance. Some of those choices will become apparent when Treasury presents its December Economic and Fiscal Update on Monday week.
This is not expected to show any significant deviation from the September pre-election update -- but it will provide the baseline from which the impact of any additional spending can be assessed.
If NZ First accepts that its extra spending should be phased in over a three-year period, then some analysts concede that it may not be as fiscally adverse as previously expected.
Operating surpluses are predicted to rise from 1997/98, because reductions in finance costs could offset increases in education and health spending.
National's formula of reducing debt faster than Labour proposes expedites this process.

The problem for NZ First is whether it will compromise some of its own ideas in order to keep the economic momentum going. For example it has called for the abandonment of the commercial principle in Crown Health Enterprises.

But the fiscal improvement expected over the next three years stems in part not just from favourable economic conditions, but also from improved operating performance from a number of crown entities, such as Housing NZ, CHEs, and Regional Health Authorities.

Some sources believe NZ First's caucus, faced with the choice of the National or Labour model on how the economy will perform, will use as a litmus test the projections on employment growth each will provide.
NZ First's president Doug Woolerton and employment spokesman Peter McCardle are said to be the influential figures who see employment as the key issue.
And for the Maori MPs, reduction of the dole queues that contain far greater numbers, proportionately, of Maoris than pakehas is also the issue that could make the difference.
(Note - The opinions expressed in this article represent the views of the author only. They should not be seen as reflecting the views of Reuters)
